<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:chart}
Let $\widetilde G:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ be a continuous cumulative distribution function
and let $I=(a,b)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an interval such that the restriction
$G=\widetilde G|_I$ is strictly increasing with
\[
\lim_{x\to a^+}G(x)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{x\to b^-}G(x)=1.
\]
Then $G:I\to(0,1)$ is called the \emph{probability coordinate chart} induced by
$\widetilde G$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:deformation}
A \emph{monotone deformation map} is a continuous non-decreasing function
$K:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $K(0)=0$ and $K(1)=1$. A monotone deformation map is
called \emph{admissible} if it is strictly increasing. We write $\mathcal K$
for the class of monotone deformation maps and $\mathcal K^\circ\subset
\mathcal K$ for the admissible ones.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:correspondence}
Let $F$ be a probability coordinate chart on the interval $I$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $K\in\mathcal K^\circ$, then $G=K\circ F$ is a probability coordinate
chart on $I$.
\item Conversely, if $G$ is a probability coordinate chart on $I$, then
$K=G\circ F^{-1}:(0,1)\to(0,1)$ extends uniquely to a map in
$\mathcal K^\circ$, and $G=K\circ F$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $K\mapsto K\circ F$ is a bijection between $\mathcal K^\circ$ and
the class of probability coordinate charts on $I$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(a) The composition $K\circ F:I\to(0,1)$ is continuous and strictly increasing
as a composition of such maps, and
\[
\lim_{x\to a^+}K(F(x))=K(0)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{x\to b^-}K(F(x))=K(1)=1 ,
\]
using the continuity of $K$ at the endpoints. Moreover $\widetilde
K\circ\widetilde G$ is a continuous distribution function on $\mathbb{R}$ whenever
$\widetilde G$ is one inducing $F$, so $K\circ F$ is induced by a distribution
function and Definition~\ref{def:chart} applies.

(b) Both $F$ and $G$ are continuous strictly increasing bijections from $I$
onto $(0,1)$, so $K=G\circ F^{-1}$ is a continuous strictly increasing
bijection of $(0,1)$ onto itself; hence
$\lim_{u\to0^+}K(u)=0$ and $\lim_{u\to1^-}K(u)=1$, and setting $K(0)=0$,
$K(1)=1$ yields the unique continuous extension, which lies in
$\mathcal K^\circ$. By construction $K\circ F=G$ on $I$. Uniqueness of the
factorization is immediate: $K$ is determined on $(0,1)$ by $K=G\circ F^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:geometry}
The factorization $G=K\circ F$ may superficially resemble a monotone
transformation of the data. The geometric reading is different, and it is the
one used in probability-coordinate geometry: a classical transformation acts in
value space, $x\mapsto g(x)$, modifying the observable; here the observable is
first transported into intrinsic probability coordinates $u=F(x)$, and the
deformation $u\mapsto K(u)$ acts \emph{inside probability space},
reallocating coordinate resolution across probability levels. The pair
$(F,K)$---not the law of $X$ alone---specifies the geometry: a single
distribution supports infinitely many probability geometries, one for each
admissible deformation of its canonical coordinates. This is the
representation-dependence of expectation emphasized in \cite{Cojocea2026a},
localized in the deformation component.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:dictionary}
A \emph{dictionary} of deformation maps is a finite collection
$\mathcal D=\{K_1,\dots,K_m\}\subset\mathcal K$. The associated convex family
is
\[
K_\lambda=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j K_j,
\qquad
\lambda\in\Delta^{m-1}
=\Bigl\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m:\lambda_j\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j=1\Bigr\}.
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:convexity}
$\mathcal K$ is convex: $K_\lambda\in\mathcal K$ for every dictionary
$\mathcal D\subset\mathcal K$ and every $\lambda\in\Delta^{m-1}$. Moreover, if
$\lambda_j>0$ for at least one index $j$ with $K_j\in\mathcal K^\circ$, then
$K_\lambda\in\mathcal K^\circ$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Convex combinations of continuous non-decreasing functions are continuous and
non-decreasing, and
\[
K_\lambda(0)=\sum_j\lambda_jK_j(0)=0,
\qquad
K_\lambda(1)=\sum_j\lambda_jK_j(1)=1 .
\]
For the second claim, if $u<v$ then
$K_\lambda(v)-K_\lambda(u)\ge\lambda_j\bigl(K_j(v)-K_j(u)\bigr)>0$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:ramp}
Let $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_n=1$ be a partition of $[0,1]$ and let
$K\in\mathcal K$ be piecewise linear with respect to this partition. For
$k=1,\dots,n$ define the \emph{ramp}
\[
H_k(u)=
\begin{cases}
0, & u\le t_{k-1},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{u-t_{k-1}}{t_k-t_{k-1}}, & t_{k-1}<u<t_k,\\[8pt]
1, & u\ge t_k.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
K(u)=\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k H_k(u),
\qquad
\lambda_k=K(t_k)-K(t_{k-1}),
\]
with $\lambda_k\ge0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k=1$. Thus every monotone
piecewise-linear deformation map lies in the convex hull of the ramp dictionary
$\mathcal H_n=\{H_1,\dots,H_n\}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Monotonicity of $K$ gives $\lambda_k=K(t_k)-K(t_{k-1})\ge0$, and the sum
telescopes to $K(1)-K(0)=1$. Let $u\in[t_{i-1},t_i]$. Then $H_k(u)=1$ for
$k<i$, $H_k(u)=0$ for $k>i$, and $H_i(u)=(u-t_{i-1})/(t_i-t_{i-1})$, so
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_kH_k(u)
=\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\lambda_k+\lambda_i\,\frac{u-t_{i-1}}{t_i-t_{i-1}}
=K(t_{i-1})+\bigl(K(t_i)-K(t_{i-1})\bigr)\frac{u-t_{i-1}}{t_i-t_{i-1}},
\]
which is the linear interpolation of $K$ on $[t_{i-1},t_i]$. Since $K$ is
piecewise linear with respect to the partition, the representation holds for
all $u\in[0,1]$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:interior}
Let $\mathcal H_n$ be the ramp dictionary of a partition
$0=t_0<\dots<t_n=1$ and let $K_\lambda=\sum_k\lambda_kH_k$,
$\lambda\in\Delta^{n-1}$. Then $K_\lambda\in\mathcal K^\circ$ if and only if
$\lambda_k>0$ for every $k$. Consequently, the admissible piecewise-linear
deformations subordinate to the partition correspond exactly to the relative
interior of the simplex $\Delta^{n-1}$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
On $(t_{k-1},t_k)$ the map $K_\lambda$ is affine with slope
$\lambda_k/(t_k-t_{k-1})$. If every $\lambda_k>0$, all slopes are positive and
$K_\lambda$ is strictly increasing. If $\lambda_k=0$ for some $k$, then
$K_\lambda$ is constant on $[t_{k-1},t_k]$ and strict monotonicity fails. The
last claim follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:ramp}, under which
$\lambda\mapsto K_\lambda$ identifies $\Delta^{n-1}$ with the monotone
piecewise-linear deformations on the partition.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Allocations on the boundary of the simplex are still monotone deformation maps
and generate monotone non-decreasing images $K_\lambda\circ F$, but these fail
strict monotonicity and are not charts: the corresponding ``geometry''
collapses entire probability intervals to single points, and the pullback
$G_\lambda^{-1}$, hence the barycenter, is undefined. The inferential theory of
\cite{Cojocea2026b} requires charts; accordingly, in everything that follows,
statements about barycenters implicitly restrict to interior allocations. This
is the precise sense in which the strictness requirement of
Definition~\ref{def:deformation} is not a technicality.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:density}
Let $K\in\mathcal K$ and let $(\pi_n)$ be a sequence of partitions of $[0,1]$
with mesh tending to zero. Let $K^{(n)}$ be the piecewise-linear interpolant of
$K$ at the nodes of $\pi_n$. Then $K^{(n)}\in\mathcal K$, and
\[
d_\infty\bigl(K^{(n)},K\bigr)\longrightarrow0 .
\]
If moreover $K\in\mathcal K^\circ$, then every $K^{(n)}\in\mathcal K^\circ$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Interpolation preserves monotonicity, endpoint values, and continuity, so
$K^{(n)}\in\mathcal K$; if $K$ is strictly increasing its nodal values are
strictly increasing, hence so is the interpolant. For the uniform convergence,
let $\omega_K$ be the modulus of continuity of $K$ (finite and vanishing at $0$
since $K$ is continuous on a compact interval). On each cell $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ of
$\pi_n$, both $K$ and $K^{(n)}$ take values in
$[K(t_{i-1}),K(t_i)]$---for $K$ by monotonicity, for $K^{(n)}$ because it
interpolates the endpoint values linearly---so
$|K^{(n)}(u)-K(u)|\le K(t_i)-K(t_{i-1})\le\omega_K(|\pi_n|)$, where $|\pi_n|$
is the mesh. Hence $d_\infty(K^{(n)},K)\le\omega_K(|\pi_n|)\to0$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:rate}
If $K\in C^2[0,1]$, the classical interpolation bound gives
\[
d_\infty\bigl(K^{(n)},K\bigr)\le\tfrac18\,\|K''\|_\infty\,|\pi_n|^2 ,
\]
so ramp interpolation on $n$ uniform cells converges at rate $n^{-2}$. This
rate is visible in the numerical study of Section~\ref{sec:numerics}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:bernstein}
Let $K\in\mathcal K$ and $n\ge1$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $B_nK\in\mathcal K^\circ$: the Bernstein approximant of \emph{any}
monotone deformation map is an admissible deformation map;
\item $d_\infty(B_nK,K)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$;
\item $B_nK$ admits the exact convex representation
\[
(B_nK)(u)=\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\,J_{n,k}(u),
\qquad
\lambda_k=K\!\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)-K\!\left(\frac{k-1}{n}\right),
\]
where
\[
J_{n,k}(u)=\sum_{j=k}^n\binom{n}{j}u^j(1-u)^{n-j}
\]
is the distribution function of the $k$-th order statistic of $n$ independent
uniform variables, i.e.\ of the $\mathrm{Beta}(k,\,n-k+1)$ law. In particular
$\{J_{n,1},\dots,J_{n,n}\}\subset\mathcal K^\circ$ is a dictionary of smooth
admissible deformation maps, and the Bernstein scheme allocates to its $k$-th
atom the same weight that Theorem~\ref{thm:ramp} allocates to the ramp on
$[\tfrac{k-1}{n},\tfrac{k}{n}]$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
(c) Since $K(0)=0$, Abel summation gives, with
$\lambda_k=K(k/n)-K((k-1)/n)$,
\[
\sum_{j=0}^nK\!\left(\frac jn\right)b_{n,j}(u)
=\sum_{j=1}^n\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^j\lambda_k\Bigr)b_{n,j}(u)
=\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\sum_{j=k}^n b_{n,j}(u)
=\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k J_{n,k}(u),
\]
where $b_{n,j}(u)=\binom nju^j(1-u)^{n-j}$. The identification of $J_{n,k}$ as
the $\mathrm{Beta}(k,n-k+1)$ distribution function is the classical
binomial--beta duality: for the $k$-th uniform order statistic one has
$\sum_{j\ge k}b_{n,j}(u)=\mathbb{P}(U_{(k)}\le u)$ \cite{ShorackWellner}. Each
$J_{n,k}$ is a polynomial with $J_{n,k}(0)=0$, $J_{n,k}(1)=1$, and derivative
$k\binom nk u^{k-1}(1-u)^{n-k}>0$ on $(0,1)$, hence
$J_{n,k}\in\mathcal K^\circ$.

(a) Endpoint interpolation gives $(B_nK)(0)=K(0)=0$ and $(B_nK)(1)=K(1)=1$.
By (c), $B_nK$ is a convex combination of the admissible maps $J_{n,k}$ with
weights $\lambda_k\ge0$ summing to $K(1)-K(0)=1$; at least one $\lambda_k$ is
strictly positive, so $B_nK\in\mathcal K^\circ$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:convexity}. (Directly:
$(B_nK)'(u)=n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl[K(\tfrac{j+1}{n})-K(\tfrac
jn)\bigr]b_{n-1,j}(u)>0$ on $(0,1)$.)

(b) is the classical uniform convergence of Bernstein polynomials for
continuous functions \cite{Lorentz1986,Rudin}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:regularization}
Part (a) deserves emphasis: even when $K$ has flat pieces---for instance a
boundary allocation $K_\lambda$ with some $\lambda_k=0$, which is not a
chart-generating map---its Bernstein approximant is strictly increasing and
therefore admissible. The Bernstein operator maps the full simplex into the
class of admissible geometries, repairing degeneracy while changing the map by
at most $d_\infty(B_nK,K)$. For smooth $K$ the price is a slower rate: by
Voronovskaya's theorem the error is of exact order $n^{-1}$
\cite{Lorentz1986}, against $n^{-2}$ for ramp interpolation
(Remark~\ref{rem:rate}). The numerical study of Section~\ref{sec:numerics}
displays both rates.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:splines}
The same construction applies to monotone spline bases: integrated M-splines
(I-splines) are non-decreasing, endpoint-normalized basis functions whose
non-negative combinations are monotone splines \cite{Ramsay1988}, and
normalized allocation vectors again produce deformation maps with the interior
corresponding to admissible geometries. Ramps are first-order I-splines; the
beta atoms $J_{n,k}$ play the analogous role in the polynomial world. Any such
system yields a finite-dimensional convex family of probability geometries
with the transfer properties of Section~\ref{sec:transfer}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:chart-transfer}
Let $F$ be a chart on $I$ and $K,\widetilde K\in\mathcal K$. Then
\[
\sup_{x\in I}\,\bigl|(K\circ F)(x)-(\widetilde K\circ F)(x)\bigr|
\;\le\;
d_\infty\bigl(K,\widetilde K\bigr),
\]
with equality when $F$ is surjective onto $(0,1)$, as it is for charts.
In particular, if $d_\infty(K^{(n)},K)\to0$ then
$K^{(n)}\circ F\to K\circ F$ uniformly on $I$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $x\in I$, $|(K\circ F)(x)-(\widetilde K\circ F)(x)|
=|K(u)-\widetilde K(u)|$ with $u=F(x)\in(0,1)$; take suprema and use the
continuity of $K-\widetilde K$ on $[0,1]$ together with the density of
$F(I)=(0,1)$ in $[0,1]$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:barycenter-stability}
Let $F$ be a chart on $I$, let $K\in\mathcal K^\circ$ with $G=K\circ F$, and
let $X$ be an $I$-valued random variable. Let $(K_n)\subset\mathcal K^\circ$
with $\varepsilon_n:=d_\infty(K_n,K)\to0$, and set $G_n=K_n\circ F$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $\bigl|\mathbb{E}[G_n(X)]-\mathbb{E}[G(X)]\bigr|\le\varepsilon_n$;
\item $G\bigl(b_{G_n}(X)\bigr)\to G\bigl(b_G(X)\bigr)$, with
$\bigl|G(b_{G_n}(X))-G(b_G(X))\bigr|\le2\varepsilon_n$;
\item $b_{G_n}(X)\to b_G(X)$;
\item if in addition $G$ is differentiable on a neighbourhood of $b_G(X)$ with
derivative bounded below by $\gamma>0$ there, then for all $n$ large enough
\[
\bigl|b_{G_n}(X)-b_G(X)\bigr|\;\le\;\frac{2\varepsilon_n}{\gamma}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
(a) $|\mathbb{E}[G_n(X)]-\mathbb{E}[G(X)]|\le\mathbb{E}|K_n(F(X))-K(F(X))|\le\varepsilon_n$.

(b) Write $m=\mathbb{E}[G(X)]$, $m_n=\mathbb{E}[G_n(X)]$, and $b_n=b_{G_n}(X)$, so that
$G_n(b_n)=m_n$ and $G(b_G(X))=m$. Then
\[
\bigl|G(b_n)-m\bigr|
\le\bigl|G(b_n)-G_n(b_n)\bigr|+\bigl|m_n-m\bigr|
\le\varepsilon_n+\varepsilon_n=2\varepsilon_n,
\]
using Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-transfer} for the first term and (a) for the
second.

(c) By \cite{Cojocea2026a}, $m\in(0,1)$, and $G^{-1}:(0,1)\to I$ is continuous
because $G$ is a continuous strictly increasing bijection. By (b),
$G(b_n)\to m$, hence $b_n=G^{-1}(G(b_n))\to G^{-1}(m)=b_G(X)$.

(d) By (c), $b_n$ eventually lies in the neighbourhood where $G'\ge\gamma$;
the mean value theorem applied to $G$ between $b_n$ and $b_G(X)$ gives
$2\varepsilon_n\ge|G(b_n)-G(b_G(X))|\ge\gamma\,|b_n-b_G(X)|$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
No differentiability, moment condition, or tail assumption on $X$ enters parts
(a)--(c): stability of the barycenter is purely a consequence of the
boundedness of probability coordinates, in line with the robustness theme of
\cite{Cojocea2026b}. Note also that the bound in (d) controls, but does not
force, the error: the actual barycenter error can be far below
$2\varepsilon_n/\gamma$ and need not decrease monotonically in $n$, since the
signed error may cross zero. Both effects are visible in
Table~\ref{tab:errors}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:moment-transfer}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:barycenter-stability}, let $r\ge1$. Then
\begin{gather*}
\bigl|\mathbb{E}[(G_n(X))^r]-\mathbb{E}[(G(X))^r]\bigr|\le r\,\varepsilon_n,
\\
\bigl|G\bigl(M_r^{(G_n)}(X)\bigr)-G\bigl(M_r^{(G)}(X)\bigr)\bigr|
\le(r+1)\,\varepsilon_n,
\end{gather*}
so $M_r^{(G_n)}(X)\to M_r^{(G)}(X)$, and under the local derivative bound of
part (d),
\[
\bigl|M_r^{(G_n)}(X)-M_r^{(G)}(X)\bigr|\le\frac{(r+1)\,\varepsilon_n}{\gamma_r}
\]
for $n$ large, where $\gamma_r>0$ lower-bounds $G'$ near $M_r^{(G)}(X)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For $s,t\in[0,1]$, $|s^r-t^r|\le r|s-t|$; hence the first bound. The remaining
claims repeat the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:barycenter-stability} with $m$
replaced by $\mathbb{E}[(G(X))^r]$ and $\varepsilon_n+r\varepsilon_n$ in place of
$2\varepsilon_n$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:quantile}
Let $X$ have continuous strictly increasing distribution function $F=F_X$
inducing a chart on $I$, and let $K\in\mathcal K^\circ$. Then
\[
b_{K\circ F}(X)
=F^{-1}\!\bigl(p_K\bigr),
\qquad
p_K=K^{-1}\!\left(\int_0^1K(u)\,du\right).
\]
Thus the barycenter of a deformed intrinsic geometry is the quantile of $X$ at
a level $p_K\in(0,1)$ determined by the deformation map alone, independently of
the law of $X$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By the uniformization property of intrinsic charts \cite{Cojocea2026a},
$U=F(X)\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, so
$\mathbb{E}[(K\circ F)(X)]=\mathbb{E}[K(U)]=\int_0^1K(u)\,du$, and
$b_{K\circ F}(X)=(K\circ F)^{-1}\bigl(\int_0^1K\bigr)
=F^{-1}\bigl(K^{-1}(\int_0^1K)\bigr)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:quantile-reading}
The identity deformation gives $p_K=1/2$: the intrinsic barycenter is the
median, consistently with the degeneracy analysis of \cite{Cojocea2026b},
whose collapse theorem shows that the fully empirical intrinsic barycenter is
asymptotically the sample median. A deformation reallocates the level: for the
ramp geometries of Section~\ref{sec:examples}, $p_\lambda=
K_\lambda^{-1}\bigl(\int_0^1K_\lambda\bigr)$ depends only on the allocation
vector $\lambda$, so selecting a geometric allocation amounts to selecting a
quantile level---early-concentrated allocations push the barycenter into the
lower quantiles, late-concentrated ones into the upper quantiles.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:moment-quantiles}
Proposition~\ref{prop:quantile} should be distinguished from the quantile
identities behind the estimators of \cite{CojoceaPele2026}: there, the
\emph{intrinsic initial moment} template
\[
M_r^{(F)}(X)=F^{-1}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[(F(X))^r]\bigr)=F^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac1{r+1}\bigr)
\]
raises the
coordinate to a power and inverts the \emph{base} chart, while here the
deformed-chart \emph{barycenter} template composes the chart with $K$ and
inverts the \emph{composition}. With the power deformation $K(u)=u^r$ the two
templates give quantile levels $\bigl(\tfrac1{r+1}\bigr)^{1/r}$ and
$\tfrac1{r+1}$ respectively. Both families are quantiles of $X$ at
distribution-free levels; the deformation calculus of this paper provides the
systematic geometry behind such identities.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
